title: Keeping sources straight
hookLine: at the first gathering Kassapa asks Ananda where each teaching was spoken; Purana keeps it as he heard it
tomorrow: what did Krishna say near the end, after all that teaching?

cards: A sunset photo, and over it in curly letters: the Buddha said. Sometimes he never said it. Buddhist tradition tells how his monks handled that problem.
After the Buddha's death, they gathered to agree on what he had actually taught. The elder Kassapa questioned Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, teaching by teaching: where was this spoken? About whom?
And Ananda named the place and the people. That's why, tradition says, the suttas open the way they do: "Thus have I heard." Then the place, and who was there.

teach.b: So every teaching came with its home: who heard it, where, and to whom it was said. But the same record holds a debate.

teach.h: PURANA: AS I HEARD IT MYSELF.
teach.b: After the gathering, a monk named Purana arrives with his own followers. Accept what the elders chanted, he's told. And Purana answers: the elders chanted it well.

But I will keep it as I heard it from the Lord himself. Two ways to name the home, both inside the tradition. The council's way says a teaching's home is the community that checked it together, word by word.

teach.h: THE COUNCIL, OR THE FIRST EAR?
teach.b: Purana's way says its home is the ear that heard it first. Each has a best case. The council guards against one memory drifting.
Purana guards against a committee smoothing out what was really said. And the Buddhist record keeps his answer right there beside the council's, which is its own kind of honesty.

teach.h: NEVER A TEACHING WITH NO HOME.
teach.b: What neither side does is let a teaching float free, with no home at all. That's the Buddhist teaching under it: a saying is handed on with its witness and its place, so the next listener can weigh it.
Today that means a small, plain habit: before you share a line, check that it has a home, a book, a teacher, a place, and hand the home on with it.

how: Buddhist suttas open with 'thus have I heard' and name the place and listeners; people who borrow the habit say whose words they're sharing, and say so when they don't know.

o: keeping your favorite books tidy and in order
knowing and naming where a teaching truly comes from
using only the newest translation of a text

games.q: the first gathering: tap the pairs.
p: asked where each teaching was spoken
named the place and the people
kept it as he heard it himself

s: 'thus have I heard' is the Buddha speaking about himself
tradition gives the words to Ananda, the one who heard; the Buddha is the one he heard.
at the gathering, Kassapa asked where each teaching was spoken and to whom
a teaching came with its place and its listeners.
every monk accepted the gathering's recitation without a word
the record keeps Purana's answer: well chanted, but I'll keep it as I heard it myself.

games.q: your book club argues: share a quote only once it's checked in the book, or as the friend who heard it remembers it? what's the best case for the second side?
o: like Purana: the one who heard it first may keep what a committee smooths out.
checking sources is pointless, since every book has mistakes in it anyway.
there isn't one; the second side is only laziness with a nice name.
games.why: Purana praised the elders' chanting but kept the teaching as he had heard it from the Buddha, and the record keeps both.

practice: Bring to mind one line that has helped you this year. Say to yourself, silently, where it lives: which book, which teacher, who told you.
If you don't know, notice that too, hold the line a little more lightly, and rest with the breath until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Keeping sources straight: handing on a teaching with its home, who said it, where, and to whom, the way the suttas begin.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: thus have I heard, the opening words of the suttas.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: name the home, the way Ananda began, thus have I heard. Goodnight for now.

sources.ref: Cullavagga XI.1 (the first council: Kassapa questions Ananda on where each teaching was spoken and about whom; Purana's answer, XI.1.11)
